If all goes according to President Obama’s plan, the United States will soon be making a major new investment of $5 billion so that other countries can help in the fight against extremists. Regardless of how sensible such a proposal might sound, many things can go wrong, and the new program already seems too heavily dependent on military responses.
Mr. Obama introduced the initiative at his West Point
commencement speech
last month, saying he would establish a network of partnerships with countries from South Asia to Africa. The goal is to train and equip foreign security forces, so they can conduct counterterrorism operations with little American involvement. The past 13 years have proved that it would be impossible, as well as unwise and unnecessary, for the United States to assume responsibility for every terrorist threat.
Terrorist threats are unquestionably out there. Despite the administration’s success at reducing the core Qaeda group behind the 9/11 attacks, Mr. Obama acknowledged that “for the foreseeable future, the most direct threat to America at home and abroad remains terrorism.” The threat has become more diffuse, involving extremists in Syria, Nigeria, Somalia, Yemen, Mali and elsewhere. The result is that while there is less likelihood of a 9/11-style attack on the United States, there is a greater danger of attacks on Americans overseas, as in Benghazi or the shopping mall in Nairobi, Mr. Obama said.
Mr. Obama said his Counterterrorism Partnerships Fund would offer expanded help to vulnerable countries, including Iraq, Lebanon and Turkey. The idea isn’t new, although Mr. Obama would greatly increase the funding beyond the millions of dollars already being spent annually. In recent years, the United States has
increasingly relied on partner countries
to help in the fight against extremists.
The Pentagon
is providing intelligence and logistics assistance to other groups, like African troops and French commandos fighting militants in Somalia and Mali. And it is also training foreign troops in countries like Niger, Yemen and Afghanistan to confront insurgents on their own territory, so American armies won’t have to.
Mr. Obama has revealed few details of his program, which must be approved by Congress and reportedly is still in the planning phase. But there are serious questions about the effectiveness of past counterterrorism efforts, and experts say the government has never systematically evaluated what works and what does not. Iraq is one cautionary example of how much can go wrong. Even though the United States spent years and
$25 billion
to build up the Iraqi Army so it could defend the country, entire units disintegrated last week in the face of assaults by Islamist insurgents, and untold amounts of valuable weapons fell into enemy hands. In another case, soldiers in
Mali overthrew
the government in March 2012, even though United States Special Operations troops had trained Malian forces.
As described by Mr. Obama, it appears that the new program is intended to be run out of the Pentagon. That would be a mistake. To be effective, the program must also address the social and political drivers of instability and involve civilians as well as military officials. For instance, training must involve not just soldiers but police officers, judges and prosecutors, with a strong emphasis on the rule of law and human rights, so cracking down on extremists does not end up radicalizing more people or empowering authoritarian leaders.
An emphasis has to be placed on good governance. There also needs to be investment in community projects, education and moderate groups that build civil society and discourage extremism. As Iraq demonstrates, just training troops to shoot and providing generals with expensive weapons will not address the threat.

Chuck Stone, whose columns for The Philadelphia Daily News denouncing racism, political corruption and police brutality inspired such trust that wanted criminals sometimes surrendered to him rather than to the police and the authorities called on him to mediate prison crises, died on Sunday in Chapel Hill, N.C. He was 89.
The death was confirmed by his daughter Krishna, who said her father had congestive heart failure. He had been a professor of journalism at the
University of North Carolina
.
Mr. Stone, who was a writer and editor for The Daily News from 1972 to ‘91, was the paper’s first black columnist and among the founders, in 1975, of the National Association of Black Journalists. He was also its first president.
Mr. Stone wrote colorful, propulsive prose with a wide range of cultural references, as likely to quote Rousseau or Abraham Lincoln as to break into the argot of black youth; he had street and statehouse cred.
His subject range
was expansive
as well — national and local politics, black history, civic and individual morality and always issues of race. Earlier in his career, when he worked for black newspapers in New York, Chicago and Washington — he covered the White House for The Washington Afro-American during the Kennedy administration — he was a fierce advocate for civil rights and black power. As a writer and editor for The New York Age, a paper based in Harlem, he befriended Malcolm X and Representative Adam Clayton Powell Jr., for whom he subsequently worked as an aide. He was fired from his job as editor in chief of The Chicago Defender when he refused to relent in his withering criticism of the city’s mayor, Richard J. Daley.
By the time he landed in Philadelphia, Mr. Stone was no less passionate, but his views had become more nuanced and independent. In the 1970s, he persistently criticized the city’s white mayor, Frank Rizzo, the former police commissioner whose department had an especially contentious relationship with the black community, and in the 1980s he persistently criticized the black mayor, Wilson Goode, for ineptitude, especially in 1985, after the mayor authorized the police bombing of a rowhouse inhabited by a radical black group known as MOVE, a calamitous event that started a destructive fire, killing 11 people, including five children.
Liberal on most social issues, Mr. Stone was in favor of the death penalty, and though he was a tenacious enemy of institutional racism, he also admonished blacks to disdain blame and seize opportunities to improve their own lives. In a 1982 column, he wrote about a coming light-heavyweight match between two local boxers, Dwight Braxton and Matthew Saad Muhammad, who had been locked up but had turned their lives around.
“I know a lot of you aren’t Dwight Braxtons or Matthew Saad Muhammads and you can’t find a job,” Mr. Stone wrote. “Hell, I’ll tell you how bad it is. Over 52 percent of all black teenagers are unemployed. ‘The world is a ghetto.’ But that’s no reason to rob a store or burglarize somebody’s home. You young brothers never think about how you would like it if another brother raped YOUR sister or burglarized YOUR home or snatched YOUR momma’s pocketbook. Black people are in terrible trouble as a race because there are not more Braxtons and Muhammads who go straight.”
Because Mr. Stone wrote so often about police corruption and brutality, crime suspects would frequently come to see him before turning themselves in, knowing that Mr. Stone would document their condition, assuring them that they wouldn’t be beaten.

In 1972, shortly after joining The News, he resolved a work stoppage by prisoners at a state prison near Wilkes-Barre. And in 1981, when a band of armed convicts took over a state prison in Graterford, holding some prison employees hostage, Gov. Richard L. Thornburgh contacted Mr. Stone, as someone the prisoners would trust as a fierce critic of the prison system, asking him to mediate the crisis. He did, successfully defusing the situation and negotiating a truce in which the hostages were freed and the prisoners were promised a transfer to a federal prison.
“I was so scared I thought I was going to cry,” Mr. Stone said.
Charles Sumner Stone Jr. was born in St. Louis on July 21, 1924. His father was a business manager for a hairdressing company, but after alcoholism overtook the father, Charles’s mother, the former Madalene Chafin, moved the family to Hartford, where Charles grew up and graduated from high school.
During World War II, he trained as a flight navigator with the Tuskegee Airmen of the Army Air Forces, though he never saw battle. Afterward, he graduated from Wesleyan University and earned a master’s degree in sociology from the University of Chicago. Before entering journalism, he worked for CARE in India and Egypt. In addition to the University of North Carolina, Mr. Stone also taught at the University of Delaware.
Mr. Stone’s early columns were collected in the volume “Tell It Like It Is.” He was also the author of “Black Political Power in America”; “King Strut,” a novel about the rise and fall of a black Congressman modeled on Powell; and a book for children, “Squizzy the Black Squirrel: A Fabulous Fable of Friendship.”
Mr. Stone was married in 1958 to Louise Davis; they divorced in 2007. Besides his daughter Krishna, he is survived by another daughter, Allegra; a son, Charles III; two sisters, Madalene Seymour and Irene Gordy; and a granddaughter.
“Chuck Stone was a product of his own design,” Elmer Smith, a member of The Daily News editorial board, wrote after Mr. Stone’s death, adding: “He didn’t study journalism. Objectivity was a polite convention that he didn’t have time for. He was a cause crusader because that’s what his people needed.”
Mr. Smith continued: “He was proudly and self-consciously black, which gave those of us who followed the confidence to be what we were and to cultivate our own distinctive voices.”

PINEHURST, N.C. — On the Pinehurst No. 2 driving range Sunday, a teenage girl shyly approached Sergio García, who greeted her with a warm embrace. She walked away as if there were clouds beneath her feet.
Lydia Ko, the third-ranked women’s player in the world, turned to her mother and said, “He hugged me.” Sighing contentedly, she extended her arms as if they were wings and said, “Don’t hug me, anybody.”
Ko, 17, was behind the range watching Phil Mickelson, a five-time major winner, pound balls with his driver when García, who was warming up for his final round of the
United States Open
, spotted her and asked to meet her. Earlier, she had crossed paths with Ernie Els, a four-time major winner.
“I can’t believe Ernie Els said hi to me,” Ko said as she set up her smartphone to take video of Mickelson’s swing.
For Ko and the other top female golfers, Sunday’s end of the men’s second major was the beginning of something novel. For the first time, the women are sharing a major course with the men. The course on which Walter Hagen, Ben Hogan and Sam Snead each won three North and South titles, and where Martin Kaymer completed a wire-to-wire win Sunday, could be the site of the American Lexi Thompson’s second major title of the year, or the first of Ko’s career. The United States Women’s Open begins Thursday at Pinehurst.
“I think, given the fact that these are back to back, it’s going to showcase, I think, just how good the females can play the game,” said Mike Davis, the executive director of the United States Golf Association.
By midafternoon, more fans were ringing the practice green than usually flock to the first tees of L.P.G.A. Tour events as the women worked on their putting alongside the men in the final pairings.
The Swede Henrik Stenson was making his way to the driving range when he passed Natalie Gulbis, a tall blonde. He gave her the once over and said to no one in particular, “The range looks so different today.”
Kaymer said he tried out one woman’s putting instructional tool on the green. Grinning, he said of the men mingling with the women: “I didn’t mind it. It relaxes the atmosphere a little bit.”
On his way to warm up, Rory McIlroy, a former world No. 1, had a brief exchange in the clubhouse with another former world No. 1, Yani Tseng, who was registering for the women’s tournament. He said he also bumped into Michelle Wie, who lives near him in Florida.
“It’s cool to run into the girls,” McIlroy said. “I would like to see it happen more often. I think it’s a good thing for women’s golf to give them a little bit more exposure.”
The face of the L.P.G.A. Tour has changed drastically in the past few years. It has gone from Annika Sorenstam’s crow’s-feet to pigtails to, now, braces. Ko and the 19-year-old Thompson are at the vanguard of a youth movement transforming the game. The competitors in this week’s tournament include Lucy Li, who is 11 and has competed at the Masters and won a trophy, albeit in the inaugural pretournament drive-chip-and-putt competition.

There remain plenty of players like Gulbis, 31, who are old enough to remember when golf was not so welcoming. Gulbis played on the boys’ team at her high school outside Sacramento because there was no girls’ squad. She competed in an L.P.G.A. Tour event at 14 and turned professional four years later. A one-time tour winner, Gulbis was the first woman to hit balls on the range alongside the men teeing off in the afternoon.
She took a back route to the range to avoid having to walk past the likes of Mickelson, García and Ian Poulter and set up at the far end, leaving several yards of space between her and the nearest PGA Tour player, the Australian Aaron Baddeley.
“It’s very intimidating being here the same time as the men,” Gulbis said.
But why? At home in Las Vegas, she is accustomed to practicing alongside Dustin Johnson, an eight-time tour winner who also works with her instructor, Butch Harmon.
“But this is the U.S. Open,” she said. “Sunday at the U.S. Open.”
The momentousness of the occasion was not lost on Gulbis, who took time between shots with her wedge to look around and drink in the scene.
“It’s Pinehurst,” she said. “This place is so rich in golf history. Just being here and seeing the pictures everywhere, it’s pretty cool. If you’re a fan of golf history, this place is awesome.”
The U.S.G.A. got the idea for having the same site host the men’s and women’s national championships from tennis, where the men and women come together at the same time and place for the majors. The difference is that there are several courts available to hold matches simultaneously at tennis’s United States Open, but only one course is in play in golf.
“You saw what it did for women’s tennis when the men and women played together,” Gulbis said. “This is a groundbreaking step for us.”
The other day, Gulbis said, she crossed paths with Kaymer in the gym. They discussed the equipment they use, and he told her what to expect from the course.
“It was fun to get some extra tips from the best players in the world,” she said.
Jessica Korda, 21, of Florida, with two victories this year, spent the morning walking outside the ropes following her father’s countryman Alex Cejka of the Czech Republic. She planned to walk inside the ropes for part of the afternoon with the final pairing of Kaymer and Rickie Fowler, with whom she had a brief conversation on the practice green.
It was not idle chitchat.
“He told me how much slower this green is than the ones they’ve been putting on,” Korda said.
After Kaymer parred the final hole to seal his eight-stroke victory, one of the first people to hug him on the green was Sandra Gal, a German whose turn to tame Pinehurst No. 2 is next.
“I hope putting them back to back works out,” Mickelson said. “There’s a lot of exciting female players that will be competing this week, and their shot selection will be interesting and their execution on such a demanding golf course will be interesting. And it’s fun to watch when you already know what the golf course is like and how it plays.”

Attention, parents of political candidates. There is now a way to spend an unlimited amount on your child’s campaign for Congress, completely ignoring that annoying $2,600 legal limit on what you can give. All you do is set up a “super PAC” for your kid and start writing checks. It’s not much harder than that 529 account you used for the same kid’s college education.
That’s what Martine Rothblatt, the founder of Sirius Satellite Radio, did for her son, Gabriel Rothblatt, who is running as a Democrat for a Florida congressional seat against a three-term incumbent. A group calling itself
Space PAC
has spent $58,000, so far, in promoting Mr. Rothblatt’s campaign. It has raised $225,000, all of it from Martine Rothblatt.
Mr. Rothblatt, trying to maintain the veneer of independence required by the law,
told USA Today
that he had no idea that the super PAC was working on his behalf until he saw some of its yard signs with his name. The issue simply has not come up in family conversations, he said. “You don’t want to, in a casual conversation, cross a line that can turn around and bite you,” he said.
Sorry, but that’s preposterous. Space PAC is no more independent from his campaign than the candidate himself. But this fictional independence is going on all over the country.
The political action committee called
Ensuring a Conservative Nebraska
raised all of its $100,000 from Rupert Dunklau, and spent most of it on behalf of Mr. Dunklau’s grandnephew Ben Sasse, the Republican nominee for the United States Senate. (Mr. Sasse
has acknowledged
that he asked his uncle to contribute to the group.) Dan Sullivan, the Republican Senate candidate in Alaska, is being supported by a super PAC called
Alaska’s Energy / America’s Values,
which has received most of its money from his family and people connected to his family’s business.
The family-financed super PACs are only the latest and most outrageous examples of how super PACs are used in this campaign cycle to evade the limits on donations. These spending groups are now a virtual requirement in competitive congressional elections. Saul Anuzis, formerly the chairman of the Michigan Republican Party, said he tells all potential candidates that they must identify generous friends and family members who can contribute to political action committees.
“It is the norm this cycle,”
he told The Washington Post
recently. “Anybody giving advice to campaigns that did not recommend super PACs as part of the strategy mix would be committing political malpractice.”
There are at least 64 super PACs dedicated to individual candidates this season, according to the Center for Responsive Politics, and they have spent more than $21 million so far on ads, polls and robocalls. Two years ago, there were 42. A majority of this year’s Senate races include a super PAC that is spending unlimited donations on behalf of a single candidate.
In many cases, the candidates are directly involved in soliciting money for the group and often have close ties to the donors and the people who decide how to spend the money. One well-known example is Senator David Vitter, a Louisiana Republican, who is the subject of a complaint to the Federal Election Commission for raising money for a super PAC, the
Fund for Louisiana’s Future
, and for employing super PAC consultants in his campaign.
Fred Wertheimer, a longtime advocate of campaign finance reform, has warned repeatedly in recent years that these groups essentially allow bribery in the form of unlimited checks. “Single-candidate super PACs can be constitutionally prohibited and must be shut down to stop the evisceration of the candidate contribution limits enacted to prevent corruption,” he said.
They could be shut down if Congress would pass the
Empowering Citizens Act
, a bill introduced in the House that would put strict limits on these kinds of coordinated contributions. But the more members of Congress depend on these groups, the less chance they will want to put a stop to them.

PARIS — At about 2:30 Tuesday afternoon, Rafael Nadal was celebrating his 28th birthday in the players’ lounge at Roland Garros.
About the same time, his Spanish countrywoman Garbiñe Muguruza won the first set of her quarterfinal against Maria Sharapova, 6-1, and another Spaniard, Carla Suárez Navarro, was ahead by two breaks, 5-2, in the first set against Eugenie Bouchard.
Two hours later, the party was over for Spain.
Sharapova rallied to beat Muguruza, 1-6, 7-5, 6-1, and Bouchard outlasted Suárez, 7-6 (4), 2-6, 7-5, to set up a French Open semifinal between Sharapova and the player often described as the next Maria Sharapova.
But that matchup did not seem likely earlier Tuesday.
Muguruza, 20, was attempting to become the first player to beat Serena Williams and Sharapova at a Grand Slam tournament, and she took advantage of Sharapova’s serving struggles to win the first set in 27 minutes.
But the match turned out to be a copy of Sharapova’s
3-6, 6-4, 6-0 victory
over Samantha Stosur in the previous round. After a sloppy first set, Sharapova grabbed control of the match by breaking Muguruza to go up by 6-5 in the second set and served out the set.
“She was doing many things well,” Sharapova said. “I also knew that the match wasn’t over. I still had a fair bit of time to change things around. You know, little by little I started playing a bit better, started getting in the court a little bit more, playing a little bit more aggressive, serving better than I did in the first set, returning as well, giving myself more looks at break points.”
She broke Muguruza again in the third game of the third set, but she had to survive an 11-minute game, saving five break points, to consolidate that break and pull away in the match.
“I need more experience in these kind of matches,” said Muguruza, ranked 35th. “I think I played very good in three sets, but in the important moments, I need to improve my mentality.”
The seventh-seeded Sharapova has emerged as the favorite in this upset-filled tournament. After years of being uncomfortable on clay, she is in the French Open semifinals for the fourth straight year, having won in 2012 and been runner-up in 2013. She is 17-1 on clay this year, winning two titles.
Bouchard, a 20-year-old Canadian, is on a streak of her own. She has won 10 matches in a row, including a run to her first WTA title in Nuremberg, Germany, the week before the French Open began. And she reached the semifinals for the second consecutive major, the only woman on the tour to do so.
“My objective is to do like Roger,” she said of Roger Federer, with a laugh. “You know, I’d like to play many semis. I have only reached two.”
Suárez, the No. 14 seed, had Bouchard down several times in the match. She served for the first set twice and was broken both times. Bouchard went on to win the set in the tiebreaker. After frustrating Bouchard in the second set, Suárez was ahead two breaks in the third, 4-1, but Bouchard went on another run.
Bouchard got one break back in the seventh game of the set, sandwiched between two holds at love. Then in the 11th game of the set, she ripped a backhand winner to go ahead by 6-5 and serve for the match. The final game included two overrules by the chair umpire, a double fault and a nervous volley into the net.
“At the end of the day, whether I win or lose, I want to at least leave it all there and try and at least battle,” Bouchard said. “I’m proud of the way I did that in both the first and third.”

MOSCOW — When the chef Jonas Grip heard that the latest Russian sanctions included banning all fish imports from Europe, he instantly called his Russian suppliers.
“I still have huge freezers from the days we used to have to bring products by truck from Sweden,” said Mr. Grip, the chef at the Scandinavia restaurant here, a Nordic cafe tucked into a leafy setting in an arched alleyway off Pushkin Square.
“I am trying to fill them again — half a ton of salmon, half a ton of whatever I need,” he said. “Everyone is going to have to live without the exclusive, imported ingredients, so I think it will be interesting, but of course it will be hard as well.”
Across this wealthy capital — where Soviet privations surrendered long ago to the spare-no-expense demands of an elite wielding significant petro-rubles — the possible ramifications of doing without sank in slowly on Friday.
Muscovites met the news with a certain equanimity. There was no sign of panicked buying of the battery of
goods the government has blocked
for one year from the European Union, Norway, the United States, Canada and Australia. Soon gone will be their beef, pork and poultry from those places, as well as seafood, dairy products, vegetables, fruits and nuts.
Supporters of the government’s instant “Buy Russian!” campaign expressed pride in helping the motherland. Government opponents, on the other hand, took the sanctions as confirmation that the country was run by dolts who thought they were punishing the West by depriving Russians of good steaks and probably raising prices.
The main television stations, all government controlled, broadcast an endless parade of earnest Russian farmers, stretching from the apple orchards in the Krasnodar territory along the northeastern Black Sea coast, to cattle ranchers on Sakhalin Island in the far east near Japan. Each farmer vowed to provide much healthier Russian fare than that foreign swill.
But in case anybody was worried about foreign goods, there were constant bulletins from Rosselkhoznadzor, the agency that regulates food imports, about deals with far-flung suppliers.
“Russian agriculture watchdog allowing fish shipments from 18 Peruvian companies,” read the headline on one such urgent dispatch.
Dmitri A. Medvedev, the prime minister, led the government cheerleading that Russians had nothing to worry about. He dredged up an old study about food security, produced four years ago when he was president, suggesting that Russia could produce everything it needed except milk and some varieties of meat.
Support for the government’s position sometimes came from unexpected quarters. Mikhail, the supply manager for a chain of Italian restaurants who, like many others interviewed did not want his full name used, said that if he needed certain spices he would get them from other countries, like India.
“We are introducing sanctions against E.U. — it serves them right,” Mikhail said, referring to the European Union. “They began it, and we responded. I think it’s fair. I would cut the gas supply to Europe, but not now. Closer to winter.”

At the opposite end was Nonna, 68, a retiree who had just shopped at Auchan, one of 82 giant French-run supermarkets across Russia. “First of all, it is Russia that is responsible for the conflict in Ukraine,” she said, clearly expressing a minority opinion on the root cause of the tit-for-tat sanctions.
As for Russia’s agricultural sanctions, “who is going to feed us?” she wanted to know. “I like good meat. I like good cheese. I like good fruit. Our agriculture is just not that developed.”
Opposition politicians mocked the idea of self-sufficiency, calling it a throwback to old attitudes that had brought the Soviet Union to collapse. “Remember how the Soviet people believed in the holy quality of Soviet cars, dishwashers and microwaves?” wrote Boris Y. Nemtsov, a former deputy prime minister, on his Facebook page.
Still, although there were jokes, nobody expected a return to the endless food lines or the empty shelves of the Soviet era. It was just a question of finding alternatives.
Mariya Kournossova, the spokeswoman for Auchan, said the chain was confident that it could replace virtually everything except certain national specialties like French Camembert.
Pundits on social media had a field day. “Vodka and caviar” was one proposal for a return to the national diet, while others suggested it was back to porridge and meatballs. There were jokes about relying on old economic allies for food like “Belarussian seafood.” (Belarus is landlocked.)
Many predicted that it was the elite who would suffer, but not the political elite, because the Kremlin has a long history of protecting its own. More likely to suffer, they say, will be the 10 percent or so who live mostly in Moscow and St. Petersburg and are critical of the government. It is they who will not be able to buy premium steaks and good cheeses. (Wine was not sanctioned.)
“It hits at the elite, but at the moment they don’t matter,” said Igor Yurgens, director of the Institute of Contemporary Development.
